Circles And Regular Triangle

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three circles fit around a triangle, and the smallest one's centre always sits straight above the point B.
How to play: Drag B along the line from A to C, or focus B and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show point names, equal angles, the square corner, or colours.
Look for the math

An 1803 temple problem hides a stubborn fact: wherever you put B on the diameter, the centre of the little circle stays directly above B. Drag B and watch the square corner refuse to change.

The question on the tablet

Start with a circle S, centre O and diameter AC, and choose a point B on AC. Circle G has diameter AB. Point E lies on S directly over the midpoint of BC, so BCE is a triangle; circle W is tucked into the curved gap between S, G and the sloping side BE. This is a Sangaku problem: prove that the line from B to the centre Q of W is perpendicular to AC. The original page links two proofs using inversion, one with negative power; here the claim is checked by computing the circle instead.

Why the triangle is isosceles

E is placed above D, the midpoint of BC, and S is centred on the same horizontal line, so E is the same distance from B and from C: BCE is an isosceles triangle. Write a = AB and c = AC. Then EB = EC = √(c(c − a)/2) while BC = c − a. Those are equal only when a = c/2, so the triangle is equilateral only when B is the midpoint of AC. The applet's name says "regular triangle", but the page states an isosceles one; the logic test confirms the title is true at that midpoint alone.

The circle in the gap

Put t = a/c. The applet places Q above B by t/(1 + t) × √(2(1 − t)) × c and gives W the radius t(1 − t)/(1 + t) × c, which simplifies to r = a(c − a)/(a + c). Three tangent contacts follow: |OQ| + r = c/2 (W touches S from inside), |PQ| = a/2 + r (W touches G from outside), and the distance from Q to the line BE is exactly r. Tick "Premise" to see the two radii drawn to the touch points and the matching angle marks at B and C.

The right angle

Q has exactly B's horizontal coordinate: it was placed straight above B. AC is horizontal, so QB and AC are perpendicular and meet at 90°. Tick "Statement" for the line QB and its two right-angle marks. The logic test compares the computation with a second transcription of the applet's own method at 604 positions of B: the angle is 90° at every one, and all three tangencies hold.

Try this: tick "Premise" and "Statement", then drag B close to A or close to C. W shrinks towards nothing, but its centre stays on the vertical through B and both right-angle marks stay square.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
